Chemical reaction

 Home Chemistry
OurBigBook.com Words: 25k Articles: 378
A chemical reaction interconverts chemical species, as defined by the [ref]. The consumed species are reactants; the formed species are reaction products. In ordinary chemical reactions, chemical atoms are rearranged while each chemical element's total atom count is conserved. For a complete chemical equation, net electric charge is conserved too.
For example, the balanced chemical equation
2H2​+O2​⟶2H2​O
(1)
describes conversion of molecular hydrogen and molecular oxygen into water. Both sides contain four hydrogen chemical atoms and two oxygen chemical atoms. Three reactant molecules become two reaction product molecules: atom counts are conserved, but molecule counts need not be. See Flowers et al., Chemistry 2e, balancing chemical equations.
The coefficients describe net consumption and formation, without asserting that three molecules collide in one step. A balanced chemical equation supplies quantitative constraints; it does not determine how quickly the chemical reaction occurs, or whether chemical equilibrium prevents complete conversion. Those questions need further information. Keeping these roles distinct makes stoichiometry useful even when the microscopic details are complicated.

Thermal decomposition

Words: 31 Articles: 1
Chemical reaction OurBigBook.com
Chemical breakdown caused by heating. A balanced chemical equation does not by itself determine the decomposition rate or every possible pathway.

Pyrolysis

Words: 12
Thermal decomposition OurBigBook.com
Chemical breakdown caused by heating, usually with little or no external oxygen supplied.

Combustion

Words: 237 Articles: 9
Chemical reaction OurBigBook.com
An exothermic chemical reaction between a fuel and an oxidizing agent. Oxygen is a common oxidizer, but neither visible flame nor oxygen is required by every broader chemical use of the term.

Taper extinction experiment

Words: 69 Articles: 1
Combustion OurBigBook.com
A controlled test in which a taper is exposed to a specified gas mixture to determine whether its candle flame persists under a fixed protocol. The result depends on composition, flow, time, taper and thermal conditions; it is not a general test of whether the gas can safely be breathed.

Carbon dioxide extinguishing concentration (xext​)

Words: 23
Taper extinction experiment OurBigBook.com
A condition-dependent carbon dioxide fraction at which a specified candle flame is extinguished in a specified protocol. Distinguish a demonstrated sufficient fraction from the least sufficient fraction.

Fuel

Words: 17
Combustion OurBigBook.com
A material used as a source of released chemical energy, commonly by reaction with an oxidizing agent during combustion.

Diffusion flame

Words: 13
Combustion OurBigBook.com
A flame in which fuel and oxidizing agent enter separately and react as they mix.

Candle flame

Words: 33 Articles: 1
Combustion OurBigBook.com
A diffusion flame sustained by the evaporation and chemical breakdown of wax delivered through a wick by capillary action.

Wick

Words: 18
Candle flame OurBigBook.com
The porous fuel-delivery component of a candle. Capillary action transports molten wax through its fibres to the region supplying gaseous fuel.

Combustibility

Words: 46 Articles: 1
Combustion OurBigBook.com
The capacity of a chemical substance to undergo combustion with a suitable oxidizing agent. It is a property, distinct from the combustible substance possessing it.

Combustible substance

Words: 27
Combustibility OurBigBook.com
A chemical substance capable of sustaining combustion with an appropriate oxidizing agent under suitable conditions. Combustibility depends on the conditions and reaction partner.
A chemical substance capable of sustaining combustion with a suitable oxidizing agent under suitable conditions.

Oxygen theory of combustion

Words: 30
Combustion OurBigBook.com
The historical explanation that ordinary combustion and metallic calcination involve combination with oxygen, rather than release of phlogiston. It should not be extended into the false claim that every chemical acid contains oxygen.

Hydration reaction

Words: 23
Chemical reaction OurBigBook.com
Addition of water to a molecular species. A carbonyl compound can form a geminal diol by hydration, distinct from a solvent hydration shell.

Salt metathesis

Words: 27
Chemical reaction OurBigBook.com
Exchange of ionic partners, often used to replace a metal halide by an anionic ligand while an alkali-metal halide forms. Atom and charge balance distinguish it from an oxidative-addition reaction.

Pericyclic reaction

Words: 307 Articles: 11
Chemical reaction OurBigBook.com
A concerted reorganization of bonding through a cyclic orbital interaction, including electrocyclic reactions. The participating orbitals and their electronic occupation determine the relevant symmetry selection rule.

Suprafacial reaction

Words: 15
Pericyclic reaction OurBigBook.com
A reaction using the same face of a participating orbital array at both reacting termini.

Sigmatropic rearrangement

Words: 12
Pericyclic reaction OurBigBook.com
A pericyclic reaction that relocates a sigma bond while reorganizing an adjacent pi system.

Cycloreversion

Words: 55 Articles: 1
Pericyclic reaction OurBigBook.com
The reverse of a cycloaddition, splitting a ring into unsaturated fragments.

Retro hetero-Diels-Alder reaction

Words: 44
Cycloreversion OurBigBook.com
A retro hetero-Diels-Alder reaction is the reverse of a Diels-Alder reaction involving a heteroatom-containing partner. For a six-membered ring with sequence O−A−B=C−D−E, cleavage of O−A and D−E can give A=B−C=D and E=O. Whether the cycloreversion is concerted or proceeds through ionic intermediates depends on the substrate and conditions.

Woodward-Hoffmann rules

Words: 34
Pericyclic reaction OurBigBook.com
Orbital-symmetry rules associated with Robert Burns Woodward and Roald Hoffmann for concerted reactions. Ground-state and photochemically excited occupations can have different allowed stereochemical modes; an allowed mode does not determine every kinetic detail or guarantee a large reaction rate.

Electrocyclic reaction

Words: 165 Articles: 5
Pericyclic reaction OurBigBook.com
Interconversion of a conjugated pi system and a ring by formation or cleavage of one sigma bond at the pi-system termini, accompanied by pi-bond redistribution. Terminal rotation connects starting geometry with product stereochemistry.

Electrocyclic ring closure

Words: 27
Electrocyclic reaction OurBigBook.com
Formation of a ring by concerted conversion of terminal pi-system overlap into a new sigma bond. Thermal four-pi closure is conrotatory, subject to the appropriate electronic-state assumptions.

Anionic eight-pi electrocyclization

Words: 17
Electrocyclic reaction OurBigBook.com
Ring closure of a seven-carbon conjugated anion with eight pi electrons; thermal orbital-symmetry selection favors disrotatory motion.

Electrocyclic selection rule

Words: 42
Electrocyclic reaction OurBigBook.com
For ordinary closed-shell systems, a thermal 4n-electron electrocyclic process is conrotatory and a thermal 4n+2-electron process is disrotatory. The corresponding simple photochemical rules are reversed. These rules relate terminal orbital phases and occupation to allowed concerted bond formation or cleavage.

Disrotatory motion

Words: 13
Electrocyclic reaction OurBigBook.com
Terminal rotation in opposite senses under a common viewing convention during an electrocyclic reaction.

Conrotatory motion

Words: 33
Electrocyclic reaction OurBigBook.com
Terminal rotation in the same rotational sense under a common viewing convention during an electrocyclic reaction. It is distinguished from disrotatory motion; looking from opposite ends without changing conventions can reverse an apparent clockwise label.

Cyclopropanation

Words: 43 Articles: 1
Chemical reaction OurBigBook.com
Formation of a three-membered carbon ring, for example by transferring a carbene-like carbon across an alkene.

Intramolecular cyclopropanation

Words: 27
Cyclopropanation OurBigBook.com
Cyclopropanation between reactive groups tethered within one molecular framework. The tether constrains approach geometry, can form an additional ring simultaneously, and can influence which alkene face reacts.

Rearrangement reaction

Words: 97 Articles: 2
Chemical reaction OurBigBook.com

Dienone-phenol rearrangement

Words: 97 Articles: 1
Rearrangement reaction OurBigBook.com
An acid-promoted skeletal migration of a cyclohexadienone followed by rearomatization to a phenol. Carbonyl protonation activates the conjugated system; migration from a suitably placed quaternary carbon and subsequent proton loss can change ring connectivity while restoring aromaticity.

Dearomatizing spirocyclization of a phenoxide

Words: 60
Dienone-phenol rearrangement OurBigBook.com
A para-tethered phenoxide can react through its carbon-nucleophilic resonance contributor. Intramolecular displacement of a tether leaving group at the para carbon creates a spiro ring and a cyclohexadienone. Subsequent acid-induced bond migration to a neighbouring carbon can expand the attached ring and restore the phenol. The two-stage sequence can therefore give a final substitution position different from the initial carbon attack.

Hydrosilylation

Words: 67 Articles: 1
Chemical reaction OurBigBook.com
Addition of Si–H across an unsaturated bond. For an alkene, the net products acquire one C–H and one C–Si bond. Alternative catalytic mechanisms can insert the alkene into either a metal–hydride or a metal–silyl bond; these alternatives should not be conflated.

Chalk-Harrod mechanism

Words: 27
Hydrosilylation OurBigBook.com
A hydrosilylation cycle involving Si–H oxidative addition, alkene insertion into the metal–hydride bond, and C–Si reductive elimination. This defines the conventional version; insertion into a metal–silyl bond describes a modified alternative.

Isomerization

Words: 18
Chemical reaction OurBigBook.com
Interconversion of isomers without changing the overall molecular formula. Conformational interconversion can be kinetically slow when rotation is hindered.

Tautomerization

Words: 17
Chemical reaction OurBigBook.com
Interconversion of constitutional forms by proton transfer accompanied by redistribution of pi bonds. Keto–enol interconversion is a familiar example.

Selectivity

Words: 47 Articles: 1
Chemical reaction OurBigBook.com
Preferential formation of one product or reaction at one site. chemoselectivity, regioselectivity and stereoselectivity describe different comparisons.

Chemoselectivity

Words: 31
Selectivity OurBigBook.com
Preferential reaction of one functional group or bond type in a molecule containing alternatives. It depends on reagents, conditions and reaction time rather than being an absolute property of a functional group.

Decarboxylation

Words: 46 Articles: 1
Chemical reaction OurBigBook.com
Loss of carbon dioxide from a compound. Malonic-acid derivatives can decarboxylate through cyclic proton-transfer/bond-cleavage arrangements that generate a carbonyl-stabilized product.

Malonic acid decarboxylation

Words: 26
Decarboxylation OurBigBook.com
Heating a substituted malonic acid can release carbon dioxide through a six-membered cyclic transition arrangement. The initial enol-like carboxylic-acid product tautomerizes to a substituted acetic acid.

Cycloaddition

Words: 168 Articles: 5
Chemical reaction OurBigBook.com
A reaction that joins unsaturated components while forming a ring and new sigma bonds. Its transition-state entropy and activation volume depend on both molecular reorganization and the surrounding medium.

Diels-Alder reaction

Words: 139 Articles: 4
Cycloaddition OurBigBook.com
A concerted cycloaddition of a conjugated diene and a dienophile that makes a six-membered ring with two new sigma bonds and one retained alkene. The internal diene atoms become the residual alkene atoms.

Diels-Alder endo preference

Words: 29
Diels-Alder reaction OurBigBook.com
A common kinetic preference for an orientation with dienophile substituents directed beneath the diene pi system. Steric and orbital interactions compete, so endo preference is not an absolute rule.

Ethylene equivalent

Words: 29
Diels-Alder reaction OurBigBook.com
A reagent combination that installs the two saturated carbons of an ethylene cycloaddition while allowing more favourable reactivity. A removable electron-withdrawing substituent can activate the dienophile and be removed later.

Endo selectivity

Words: 32
Diels-Alder reaction OurBigBook.com
A preference for the cycloaddition orientation in which relevant dienophile substituents lie under the diene framework in the transition geometry. It is distinct from regiochemistry and is not an unconditional guarantee of one product.

Dienophile

Words: 21
Diels-Alder reaction OurBigBook.com
The unsaturated partner that combines with a conjugated diene in a Diels–Alder reaction. Electron-withdrawing substituents often enhance reactivity in a normal-electron-demand process.

Mesylation

Words: 24
Chemical reaction OurBigBook.com
Mesylation installs a methanesulfonyl group on a heteroatom, often alcohol oxygen. An alcohol attacks electrophilic sulfur of a sulfonylating reagent, and base removes the O–H proton.

Hydroalumination

Words: 36 Articles: 1
Chemical reaction OurBigBook.com
Hydroalumination adds an Al–H equivalent across an unsaturated bond. Syn and directed trans pathways give different alkenyl-aluminium geometries; protonolysis can preserve that stereochemical information.

Directed trans-hydroalumination

Words: 13
Hydroalumination OurBigBook.com
Oxygen-directed anti addition of aluminium and hydrogen across an alkyne, giving a stereodefined vinylaluminium species.

Dihydroxylation

Words: 38 Articles: 1
Chemical reaction OurBigBook.com
Dihydroxylation installs hydroxyl groups on adjacent alkene carbons. osmium tetroxide gives a syn addition pathway through a cyclic osmate ester.

Cyclic osmate ester

Words: 26
Dihydroxylation OurBigBook.com
A cyclic osmate ester contains the newly formed carbon–oxygen bonds of an osmium-mediated alkene dihydroxylation. Both oxygen atoms attach on the same face; hydrolytic cleavage of metal–oxygen bonds releases the diol.

Transacetalization

Words: 22
Chemical reaction OurBigBook.com
Transacetalization exchanges acetal alkoxy groups through acid-catalyzed cleavage and reformation. Protonated alkoxy departure gives an oxocarbenium species that a new alcohol can capture.

Syn addition

Words: 19
Chemical reaction OurBigBook.com

oxidation of an enol or enolate can generate a carbon-centred radical that adds intramolecularly to an alkene. Further oxidation or oxygen capture determines the final functional group.

Precipitation (chemistry)

Words: 3k Articles: 15
Chemical reaction OurBigBook.com
Precipitation is formation of a solid from a chemical solution; the formed solid is a precipitate. Dissolved chemical species enter a separate thermodynamic phase. A newly formed solid can create a surface for heterogeneous catalysis; observing it does not establish the composition or catalytic role of that surface.
For example, mixing suitable chemical solutions of calcium chloride and sodium carbonate can form calcium carbonate:
Ca2+(aq)+CO32−​(aq)⟶CaCO3​(s).
(2)
Here aq means dissolved in water, and s marks the solid. Both sides contain one calcium chemical atom, one carbon chemical atom, and three oxygen chemical atoms; net electric charge is +2−2=0 on the left and zero on the right. The arrow describes the net change when precipitation occurs, rather than promising complete removal of either ion. The calcium carbonate precipitation experiment makes this phase separation visible.[ref]
The attraction is that an invisible dissolved inventory becomes a recoverable solid. Net ionic equations track that transfer; the saturation criterion for precipitation determines whether it is favored under specified conditions. This combination supports separations and chemical analysis.[ref]

Net ionic equation

Words: 237 Articles: 1
Precipitation (chemistry) OurBigBook.com
A net ionic equation retains the chemical species changed by a chemical reaction and cancels spectator ions present unchanged on both sides. Dissolved strong electrolytes are represented by their separated ions, while a solid product retains its chemical formula. Cancellation preserves both elemental inventories and electric charge conservation.[ref]
For the calcium carbonate example, the complete ionic account is
​Ca2+(aq)+2Cl−(aq)+2Na+(aq)+CO32−​(aq)⟶CaCO3​(s)+2Na+(aq)+2Cl−(aq).​
(3)
Canceling the sodium cations and chloride anions yields the net ionic equation above. Neither cancellation nor the conventional sodium chloride formula implies that the remaining dissolved ions have become paired molecules.
For this schematic, let ξ be the amount of substance of AB formed. With no competing chemical reactions or losses,
nA,aq​=nA,0​−ξ,nB,aq​=nB,0​−ξ,nAB,s​=ξ,0≤ξ≤min(nA,0​,nB,0​).
(4)
Adding each dissolved inventory to its contribution in the solid recovers its initial total. Each dissolved pair has net electric charge zero, so transferring a pair into neutral AB also preserves electric charge conservation. This is a short stoichiometry argument; choosing the actual ξ additionally needs chemical equilibrium or chemical kinetics information.

Spectator ion

Words: 37

A spectator ion cancels from the chosen net ionic equation because its net inventory is unchanged. This label does not make it physically irrelevant: dissolved spectator ions contribute to ionic strength, which affects activity coefficients. Their concentrations can also change during dilution even though their amount of substance remains fixed.

Solubility product (Ksp​)

Words: 2k Articles: 8
Precipitation (chemistry) OurBigBook.com
The solubility product is the equilibrium constant for dissolution of a specified solid into its dissolved ions. For a pure bulk AB solid at the chosen temperature, pressure and standard states,
AB(s)⇌A+(aq)+B−(aq),Ksp​=aA​aB​.
(5)
The pure bulk solid's thermodynamic activity is one in this convention. Coexisting solid and chemical solution at chemical equilibrium give this equality. If all available solid dissolves, the final chemical solution may instead be undersaturated; do not impose equality merely because a salt was initially added.[ref]
Using the thermodynamic activity definition ai​=γi​ci​/c∘, with activity coefficients γi​ and reference molar concentration c∘, gives the independent conversion
Ksp​=γA​γB​(c∘)2cA​cB​​,Ksp,c​=γA​γB​Ksp​(c∘)2​.
(6)
Thus Ksp​ is dimensionless, while the conditional concentration form Ksp,c​ has units M2 for this one-to-one model. Treating Ksp,c​ as constant requires a justified fixed or approximately fixed activity coefficient product. Changing ionic strength can change that product even at fixed temperature; changing temperature can change the equilibrium constant itself. Specify the solid thermodynamic phase too: different crystal polymorphs need not have the same solubility product.

Solubility product OurBigBook.com
The molar solubility s is the amount of substance of a specified solid dissolved per volume of saturated chemical solution, under stated conditions. It counts dissolved formula units, not the sum of all dissolved ion concentrations. For AB with no initial A or B and no competing chemical reactions, one-to-one stoichiometry gives cA​=cB​=s. For an AB2​ solid, the corresponding concentrations are s and 2s.[ref]

Solubility product and material balance

Words: 401
Solubility product OurBigBook.com
A solubility product constrains a product of thermodynamic activities; the available inventories determine which combinations of concentrations are possible. Their intersection determines the molar solubility. Consider an original, abstract AB solid, with the preceding one-to-one dissolution chemical equation. Stipulate c∘=1M, γA​=γB​=1 and Ksp,c​=10−4M2 at fixed temperature and pressure. Thus Ksp​=10−4 is dimensionless. These are chosen model parameters, not data for an identified material.
Initially, a completely dissociated soluble XB salt supplies B anions at molar concentration c0​≥0 and X cations at the same molar concentration; A is absent. All three ions have unit electric charge magnitude. X remains a spectator ion, and only AB can form a solid. Assume constant volume, no additional chemical reactions, and negligible contributions from self-ionization of water. Dissolving AB raises both reacting-ion concentrations by the same s:
cA​=s,cB​=c0​+s,cX​=c0​.
(7)
Charge neutrality is satisfied: cA​+cX​−cB​=s+c0​−(s+c0​)=0. Adding B alone without its accompanying cation would omit the initial electric charge balance.
In the plane of the two reacting-ion concentrations, this inventory constraint is the line cB​=cA​+c0​. Saturation supplies the hyperbola cB​=Ksp,c​/cA​ for cA​>0. Their positive intersection solves a quadratic equation:
s(s+c0​)=Ksp,c​,s∗​=2c02​+4Ksp,c​​−c0​​=c02​+4Ksp,c​​+c0​2Ksp,c​​.
(8)
The quadratic formula supplies two roots of a polynomial; only the positive one is a physical concentration. Uniqueness also follows because s(s+c0​) strictly increases for s≥0, starting at zero and growing without bound. The second expression, obtained by multiplying by the conjugate, avoids subtraction of nearly equal numbers at large c0​.
For pure water, c0​=0 gives s∗​=Ksp,c​​=0.010M. For c0​=0.030M,
s∗​≈0.003027756M,cB​≈0.033027756M.
(9)
Their product is 10−4M2, although neither concentration equals the pure-water value. This is the useful geometrical distinction: an inventory line and an equilibrium constant specify different constraints.
Check the solid inventory before imposing saturation. If the initially added AB has amount of substance n0​ in volume V, the saturated branch requires n0​>Vs∗​ for excess solid to remain. For example, choose n0​=0.0020mol and V=0.100L. In pure water, 0.0010mol dissolves and the same amount of substance remains as solid. At c0​=0.030M, approximately 0.0003027756mol dissolves, leaving 0.0016972244mol as solid. In this model, an insufficient supply instead gives
s=min{n0​/V,s∗​}.
(10)
If n0​/V<s∗​, all AB dissolves and the ion product is below the solubility product. At n0​/V=s∗​, the last solid disappears exactly at saturation.

Common-ion effect

Words: 313
Solubility product OurBigBook.com
The common-ion effect is the change in a chemical equilibrium caused by adding an ion already participating in it. In the fixed-activity coefficient AB model, adding the common B anion lowers the molar solubility. The shared ion participates regardless of which salt supplied it.[ref]
The preceding solubility product and material balance give a short proof without a qualitative slogan. Taking a derivative of s∗2​+c0​s∗​=Ksp,c​ at fixed Ksp,c​ gives
(2s∗​+c0​)dc0​ds∗​​+s∗​=0,dc0​ds∗​​=−2s∗​+c0​s∗​​<0.
(11)
Thus the molar solubility decreases continuously as c0​ increases. At c0​=0, the derivative is −1/2; for a very large common-ion background, the rationalized expression approaches Ksp,c​/c0​. The solubility product is fixed within this model even while the molar solubility changes.
Neglecting s∗​ beside c0​ replaces s∗​(c0​+s∗​)=Ksp,c​ by c0​sapp​=Ksp,c​. This approximation always overestimates the exact molar solubility, since it neglects the B anions supplied by AB itself. For c0​>0, its relative error has an exact simple form:
sapp​=c0​Ksp,c​​=s∗​+c0​s∗2​​,s∗​sapp​−s∗​​=c0​s∗​​.
(12)
At c0​=0.030M, sapp​=0.003333333M, approximately 10.1% too high. At c0​=0.100M, s∗​=0.000990195M and sapp​=0.001000000M, approximately 0.990% too high. A small solubility product by itself does not justify the approximation: the common-ion background must be large compared with the resulting molar solubility.
For a desired fractional relative error at most ε>0, substituting s∗​/c0​≤ε into the exact balance gives the equivalent criterion
c0​≥ε(1+ε)Ksp,c​​​.
(13)
For this model, a 5% tolerance requires c0​≥0.0436436M. This bound concerns only the algebraic approximation. In a real chemical solution, changes in ionic strength and activity coefficients, or competing chemical reactions, can invalidate a constant Ksp,c​ even when this bound is met.

Solubility product measurement by titration

Words: 351
Solubility product OurBigBook.com
How can an invisible dissolved inventory be measured? The unsigned laboratory handout Solubility Product Constant, Ksp, for Calcium Hydroxide by Acid-Base Titration, Procedure, starts with saturated calcium hydroxide, supplied by the teacher or prepared from calcium and water. Its apparatus includes filter paper, a funnel, stoppered flasks, a volumetric pipette, a volumetric flask and a burette. Two successive rounds of filtration remove particles. The filtrate is stoppered to reduce carbon dioxide exposure. A 10.00mL aliquot is diluted with deionized water and titrated with standardized hydrochloric acid; bromothymol blue gives a pale-green titration endpoint. The readout is the difference between final and initial burette readings; four consistent trials are required.[ref]
Unlike AB, calcium hydroxide has one-to-two dissolution stoichiometry:
Ca(OH)2​(s)⇌Ca2+(aq)+2OH−(aq),Ksp,c​=[Ca2+][OH−]2.
(14)
For molar solubility s in the ideal model with no background calcium or hydroxide, no additional chemical reactions, and negligible self-ionization of water, [Ca2+]=s and [OH−]=2s. Hence Ksp,c​=4s3, with units M3; it is not the AB constant used in the figures. The neutralization chemical equation is H++OH−⟶H2​O. Let CH​ be the known titrant molar concentration, v its delivered volume at the equivalence point, and Va​ the original aliquot volume. Then the inventory calculation is
h=[OH−]=Va​CH​v​,s=2h​,Ksp,c​=2h3​.
(15)
Dilution of the aliquot changes its concentration during the acid-base titration, but preserves its initial amount of substance of hydroxide. Therefore Va​, rather than the diluted flask volume, belongs in the denominator.
The handout identifies two biases: carried-over calcium hydroxide solid dissolves during acid-base titration, consuming extra titrant; carbon dioxide consumes hydroxide and forms calcium carbonate. Filtration and stoppering address these effects, while repeat trials test consistency. Its review questions also ask about dissolved ion pairs, which filtration cannot remove.[ref]
Further controls would compare a water blank, independently verify titrant standardization, and record the saturation temperature; these are proposed checks, not reported measurements. A titration endpoint estimates the equivalence point and may introduce a systematic offset. Even perfect inventory measurement does not determine activity coefficients. Recovering the dimensionless thermodynamic solubility product additionally requires
Ksp​=γCa​γOH2​(c∘)3Ksp,c​​.
(16)
This explains both the power and the limit of the experiment: acid-base titration measures a dissolved inventory, while the link from that inventory to a thermodynamic equilibrium constant still depends on a chemical model.

Solubility product OurBigBook.com
The ion product evaluates the same dissolved-ion thermodynamic activity product as the solubility product, but at the current composition rather than necessarily at chemical equilibrium. For AB, Qsp​=aA​aB​; its concentration counterpart is Qc​=cA​cB​. Compare Qc​ with Ksp,c​ only under compatible activity coefficient assumptions.[ref]
For other stoichiometries, use the dissolution coefficients as powers: AB2​(s)⇌A2+(aq)+2B−(aq) gives Qsp​=aA​aB2​. A solubility product is not itself the molar concentration dissolved; even in the ideal AB model in pure water, that concentration is Ksp,c​​.

Saturation criterion for precipitation (Qsp​≷Ksp​)

Words: 149 Articles: 1
Solubility product OurBigBook.com
Relative to the specified solid, Qsp​<Ksp​ favors dissolution if that solid is available; Qsp​>Ksp​ favors precipitation; equality marks saturation. These comparisons identify a driving direction favored by thermodynamics, not a reaction rate.[ref]
A proof outline comes from the reaction Gibbs free energy for dissolution:
Δr​G=RTln(Ksp​Qsp​​).
(17)
Here R is the molar gas constant and T>0 the absolute temperature. If Qsp​>Ksp​, the logarithm is positive, making the reverse transfer into solid favorable. At equality the bulk driving difference vanishes. Equality can also occur at the boundary where the last solid disappears, but it is not a universal constraint on every solid-free chemical solution.
Supersaturated solution
Words: 50
Saturation criterion for precipitation OurBigBook.com
A supersaturated solution has an ion product above the relevant solubility product. It can persist through metastability: nucleation must first create a sufficiently large new solid region. Added surfaces, impurities and mixing history can affect that barrier. Therefore a clear sample during a finite observation does not prove undersaturation, and visible cloudiness does not measure the ion product.

Solubility product OurBigBook.com
Consider an original toy AB salt model with Ksp,c​=10−8M2 stipulated at fixed temperature and fixed activity coefficient product. This is a conditional concentration constant, not measured data for calcium carbonate or any identified material. A stock contains A cations and X anions; another contains Y cations and B anions. All four ions have unit electric charge magnitude. Only AB can form a solid; X and Y remain spectator ions. Assume full dissociation, no other chemical reactions, and a mixed volume equal to the sum of the initial volumes.
Mix two stocks, each of volume V,, each at molar concentration C of its indicated salt. Before any precipitation, the mixed volume is 2V, so
cA,0​=cB,0​=2VCV​=2C​,Qc,0​=4C2​.
(18)
Multiplying the two stock concentrations would overestimate the mixed ion product by a factor of four. The saturation threshold is C=2Ksp,c​​=2×10−4M.
If C=10−4M, mixing gives Qc,0​=2.5×10−9M2<Ksp,c​: no AB precipitate is favored. If C=4×10−4M, mixing gives Qc,0​=4×10−8M2>Ksp,c​. cA,eq​=cB,eq​=Ksp,c​​=10−4M,2VnAB,s​​=2C​−10−4M=10−4M.
(19)
For two 10mL portions in the second case, each reacting ion starts with 4μmol; the final 20mL chemical solution retains 2μmol of each, and 2μmol of AB enters the solid. The respective X and Y inventories stay at 4μmol. Exactly half of each reacting inventory precipitates in this toy model.

(20)
When x>0, the last condition requires saturation; when x=0, the inventory can leave an undersaturated chemical solution. Together these give x=max{0,C/2−Ksp,c​​}. This excludes a persistent supersaturated solution by its explicit chemical equilibrium assumption; it does not model a nucleation delay.

Calcium carbonate precipitation experiment

Words: 216
Precipitation (chemistry) OurBigBook.com
The University of Utah's teaching module Carbon Captured Chalk by Tony Butterfield describes a supervised demonstration. Its Materials and Methods uses a balance, weighing boats, spatula, separate centrifuge tubes, a volume-measuring vessel and filter paper. Sodium carbonate and calcium chloride are dissolved separately in water before mixing. The reported readout is an initially opaque mixture followed by a milky dispersion of fine solid particles; filtration retains the chalk-like product, which is then dried. The module also proposes observing drops together on a slide using an optical microscope.[ref]
The handout does not report blank trials. Useful additional controls would retain each starting chemical solution separately, mix each with water, and pass water alone through the same filter. A new solid only in the combined sample would support a mixing-dependent chemical reaction; these are proposed comparisons, not reported results. Residue from a filter blank would instead flag contamination.
Cloudiness plus a retained solid supports phase separation; appearance alone cannot establish composition, a particular crystal polymorph, quantitative yield or the solubility product. Fine solid particles may pass through a filter, and retained liquid can leave dissolved salts on drying. Identifying calcium carbonate needs additional chemical or structural evidence. The teaching source supplies no measured ion products, instrument-calibrated cloudiness series or equilibration test. Its concentrated demonstration therefore illustrates precipitation without validating the toy model's conditional constant or proving complete removal of dissolved calcium.

Redox

Words: 3k Articles: 34
Chemical reaction OurBigBook.com
A redox chemical reaction couples oxidation and reduction. In the electrode examples here, oxidation releases electrons and reduction accepts them. [ref]
Redox can be recognized by changes in oxidation state: an increase records oxidation, a decrease reduction. These are formal electron assignments, distinct from measured partial atomic charges. Half-reactions expose the matching loss and gain, making electric charge conservation visible.[ref]
The electron accounting need not describe free electrons travelling between spatially separated chemical species. For example, in 2H2​+O2​⟶2H2​O, hydrogen changes from oxidation state 0 to +1 and oxygen from 0 to −2. Four hydrogen chemical atoms lose four formally assigned electrons in total; two oxygen chemical atoms gain four. The water product has covalent bonds, and these assignments do not turn it into separated ions. See ionic approximation of bonds and electron transfer and ionic character.
By contrast, neutralization can rearrange chemical bonds without changing oxidation states:
H+(aq)+OH−(aq)⟶H2​O(l).
(21)
Hydrogen remains +1 and oxygen remains −2. The aqueous proton notation abbreviates its interaction with water. This acid-base chemistry example conserves electric charge but has no matching increase and decrease of oxidation state; movement of ions or a change of chemical bonds alone does not establish redox.

Redox electron balance (ne,lost​=ne,gained​)

Words: 396
Redox OurBigBook.com
Consider the reacting zinc and copper species in the zinc-copper displacement experiment. Split the net chemical equation into two half-reactions:
oxidation:reduction:​Zn(s)⟶Zn2+(aq)+2e−,Cu2+(aq)+2e−⟶Cu(s).​
(22)
The zinc oxidation state rises from 0 to +2; the copper oxidation state falls from +2 to 0. Add the half-reactions: two released electrons match two accepted electrons. Cancelling 2e− from both sides gives[ref]
Zn(s)+Cu2+(aq)⟶Zn2+(aq)+Cu(s).​
(23)
Thus the closed net chemical reaction has zero net production of free electrons. Cancellation does not destroy electrons: it removes a matched internal exchange from the written chemical equation. The half-reactions alone are incomplete descriptions of the whole reacting system. In a galvanic cell, the exchange can pass through a wire; in the zinc-copper displacement experiment, the reacting materials meet at the same metal surface. The equations do not require a reservoir of free electrons in the bulk chemical solution.
Check both kinds of balance. The oxidation line has net electric charge 0 on the left and (+2−2)e=0 on the right; the reduction line has (+2−2)e=0 on the left and 0 on the right. The net chemical equation contains one zinc and one copper chemical atom on each side and has net electric charge +2e on each side, where e is the positive elementary charge. The written reacting species need not be electrically neutral as a group: the bulk chemical solution also contains compensating anions.
There is an even more literal check. Zinc has atomic number 30 and copper 29, so the initial pair contains 30+(29−2)=57 electrons. The final pair contains (30−2)+29=57 electrons. Only their distribution has changed. Conserved chemical element counts give the usual chemical mass conservation inventory; changing the counts of neutral and charged species does not create or remove their atomic nuclei.
Matching electrons is necessary but does not replace balancing every chemical element. The acidic permanganate-iron balance illustrates unequal one- and five-electron exchanges, with water and protons also needed. Conversely, a balanced chemical equation alone establishes neither a reaction rate nor a detailed mechanism. Its usefulness is that it fixes the stoichiometry even when those additional questions remain open.

Redox OurBigBook.com
An inspected university demonstration makes the paired changes visible. The 2021 Chemical Demonstrations Booklet hosted by Edith Cowan University describes two cut square zinc strips, each immersed in a separate glass beaker. One contains blue copper(II) sulfate chemical solution, the other colourless zinc sulfate chemical solution. The published readouts are the appearance of a brown copper deposit on the first strip and fading of its blue chemical solution; after thirty minutes more deposit is reported. The comparison strip in zinc sulfate shows no visible change. The documented preparation is cutting the strips; surface polishing is not specified.[ref]
The reported interpretation is conversion of dissolved Cu2+ to metallic copper, accompanied by conversion of metallic zinc to dissolved Zn2+. The sulfate anions balance bulk electric charge and cancel from the net chemical equation. The comparison shows that merely immersing a zinc strip in a sulfate chemical solution does not reproduce the visible coating.[ref]
Appearance is evidence for the proposed conversion, rather than a quantitative measurement of the two-electron ratio. Fading alone could also reflect dilution; deposit colour alone does not independently establish its composition. A stronger follow-up would compare the copper content of the chemical solution before and after, identify the solid, and check dissolved zinc. These are proposed analytical checks, not results reported in the booklet. Comparable starting chemical solutions, surface condition, immersion and observation time help interpret a comparison; an unchanged-looking strip does not rule out slow or invisible chemical reactions.
The two-electron interpretation comes from the species identities and electric charge balance, supported by the paired observations. It does not imply that the coating's mass equals the mass of zinc consumed: the same amount of substance of different chemical elements generally have different molar masses. Nor does it resolve microscopic surface sites or reaction pathways. The same net redox can be organized into separated compartments in a Daniell cell to obtain electrical work.

An oxidation state is an electron-bookkeeping assignment to a chemical atom: its electric charge number after the ionic approximation of bonds. It helps identify oxidation and reduction and determine stoichiometry, even for covalent bonds without separate charged ions. In water, each hydrogen has oxidation state +1 and oxygen has −2; this does not assert that a water molecule contains two free protons and a free oxide ion.[ref]
Three conventions answer different questions. Formal charge divides each bonding electron pair equally in a chosen Lewis structure. Oxidation state uses the ionic approximation of bonds. Partial atomic charge instead partitions the actual electron density and depends on that partition. In the ordinary water Lewis structure, every formal charge is zero although the oxidation states are not. Neither bookkeeping convention supplies numerical partial atomic charges.

For the routine examples here, assign all bonding electrons between different chemical elements to the more electronegative partner; divide bonding electrons between identical chemical elements equally. Retain each lone pair on its original chemical atom. Subtract the assigned valence electron count Niassigned​ from the neutral chemical atom's valence electron count vi​. The IUPAC convention uses Allen electronegativity, based on free-chemical atom valence electron energies. Close electronegativity comparisons and some reversibly bound chemical compounds require care beyond this simple rule.[ref]
The examples explain exceptions to memorized rules:
  • Water, H−O−H: oxygen receives both O–H bond pairs plus its two lone pairs, giving eight assigned valence electrons and 6−8=−2. Each hydrogen receives none, giving 1−0=+1.
  • Hydrogen peroxide, H−O−O−H: each oxygen receives its O–H bond pair, one electron from O–O, and four electrons in lone pairs. Thus each has 6−7=−1, while each hydrogen remains +1. The O–O connection is why the usual −2 oxygen shortcut fails.
  • Molecular oxygen, O2​: equal splitting of the O–O bonding electrons leaves each oxygen assigned six valence electrons, so each has oxidation state zero.
  • Sodium hydride, NaH: hydrogen is more electronegative than sodium. The formula unit is assigned sodium +1 and hydrogen −1, consistent with the hydrogen anion. The usual +1 hydrogen shortcut fails here.
These drawings record allocations, not molecular geometry or a physical process of breaking the chemical bonds. In particular, the O–O line in the molecular oxygen panel only marks the connection; it does not assert a complete Lewis structure or spin state.
Oxidation state sum rule (∑i​OSi​=z)
Words: 111
Oxidation state OurBigBook.com
Sum oxidation states over all chemical atoms of the specified molecule, ion or formula unit, including multiplicities:
∑i​OSi​=z,q=ze.
(24)
Here q is the net electric charge and e the positive elementary charge. For a neutral entity the sum is zero; for an ion it equals its signed electric charge number z. The reason is simple: the allocation assigns every valence electron exactly once, so the sum is the neutral electron budget minus the actual electron count.
For water, 2(+1)+(−2)=0; for hydrogen peroxide, 2(+1)+2(−1)=0. In permanganate, MnO4−​, assigning each oxygen −2 gives x+4(−2)=−1, so manganese has oxidation state +7. This is not a free Mn7+ ion: the entire permanganate anion has net electric charge −e. The sum rule supplies a constraint; without additional assignments it cannot determine every individual oxidation state.
Acidic permanganate-iron balance
Words: 225
Oxidation state OurBigBook.com
An increase in oxidation state records oxidation; a decrease records reduction. Thus Fe2+→Fe3+ raises the iron oxidation state by one, while MnO4−​→Mn2+ lowers the manganese oxidation state from +7 to +2. Five iron ions supply the five-electron inventory required per permanganate ion.
In an acidic chemical solution, the complete half-reactions are
Fe2+MnO4−​+8H++5e−​⟶Fe3++e−,⟶Mn2++4H2​O.​
(25)
First balance oxygen with four water molecules, then hydrogen with eight protons, and finally electric charge with five electrons. Multiply the iron half-reaction by five and add; the exchanged electrons cancel:
MnO4−​+8H++5Fe2+⟶Mn2++4H2​O+5Fe3+.​
(26)
Both sides contain one manganese, four oxygen, eight hydrogen and five iron chemical atoms, with net electric charge +17e. The H+ notation represents the acidic aqueous proton inventory; it does not imply bare protons moving independently of water. These half-reactions and their sum are the acidic balance used in the documented permanganate-iron titration.[ref]
The coefficients predict amounts consumed, not a collision of five ions or an elementary reaction. Bulk chemical solution also contains compensating counterions, which are omitted from this net chemical equation. The hydrogen and oxygen oxidation states are unchanged; balancing their inventories remains essential even though they do not account for the exchanged electrons.

Redox titration

Words: 1k Articles: 2
Redox OurBigBook.com
A redox titration adds a measured amount of substance of one reactant to determine another through a known redox chemical equation. The burette reading becomes an amount through concentration; the balanced chemical equation supplies the amount ratio. A colour endpoint additionally needs a chemical explanation, as in the permanganate-iron titration.
The useful bridge is an electron inventory. If each sample entity supplies zA​ electrons and each titrant entity accepts zT​, matching the formal exchanged amount of substance of electrons gives
zA​nA​=zT​nT​,nA​=zA​zT​​cT​Veq​.
(27)
Here cT​ is the titrant molar concentration and Veq​ the volume attributable to the sample at the equivalence point. These are net half-reaction counts, not a claim that free electrons accumulate in the flask. The redox conversion must be sufficiently complete and selective for the stated stoichiometry to identify nA​.
This is why a small visible signal can reveal a much larger invisible inventory: the signal locates a stopping point, while titrant standardization and stoichiometry turn delivery into amount of substance. The titration endpoint estimates the equivalence point; repeatable colour alone establishes neither correct titrant concentration nor chemical selectivity. The permanganate-iron endpoint and blank model separates these assumptions.

Permanganate-iron titration

Words: 860 Articles: 1
Redox titration OurBigBook.com
A proposed modern teaching measurement puts a pipette-measured portion of an iron Fe2+ chemical solution in a conical flask, acidifies with excess dilute sulfuric acid, and adds standardized potassium permanganate from a clamped burette while swirling. The documented endpoint principle is that added purple permanganate is consumed until the first small excess leaves a pale purple colour; no separate colour indicator is required. Insufficient acidity can produce brown manganese dioxide, invalidating the assumed five-electron half-reaction.[ref]
Record initial and final burette readings; their difference is the delivered volume V. The following controls are proposed additions to test the inference. Run a reagent blank with the same water, sulfuric acid and endpoint criterion but no sample, obtaining Vb​. Use a separately established potassium permanganate concentration c, clear the burette tip of air, and repeat sample portions. A known added amount of substance of Fe2+ should increase consumption by one fifth of that amount. A blank estimates reagent demand and the small endpoint excess; it cannot remove an interfering sample reactant.
Assuming complete, selective reaction according to the acidic permanganate-iron balance, the corrected inference is
n(Fe2+)=5c(V−Vb​).
(28)
With c in molL−1, use V and Vb​ in litres. As an original stipulated calculation, not an experimental result, take c=0.02000molL−1, V=12.60mL and Vb​=0.10mL. Then the permanganate consumption is 0.2500mmol and the inferred Fe2+ amount is 1.250mmol. In a 25.00mL sample portion this corresponds to 0.05000molL−1.
In this example the corrected volume is 12.50mL=0.01250L. The acidic permanganate-iron balance gives zA​=1 for Fe2+ and zT​=5 for permanganate. Thus 0.2500mmol of permanganate accepts 1.250mmol of formal electrons, exactly what 1.250mmol of Fe2+ supplies. The amount of substance ratio is five to one, despite equality of the exchanged electron amounts.
The denominator is the original 25.00mL aliquot, not its final volume after adding sulfuric acid, water and titrant. Such dilution changes concentrations in the flask without changing the initial sampled amount of substance of Fe2+. Omitting the 0.10mL titration blank would instead give 1.260mmol and 0.05040molL−1, an overestimate of 0.80% relative to the corrected constructed value. The displayed digits express the stipulated calculation, rather than establish its measurement uncertainty.
The endpoint detects residual permanganate, not the iron identity directly. Other sample reactants that consume permanganate raise the apparent Fe2+ amount; prior oxidation of sample Fe2+ to Fe3+ lowers it. A recovery check probes response to the added iron but does not prove absence of every interference. The readout determines the reacting Fe2+ inventory under the stated conditions, rather than total iron in an arbitrary mixture. No measured titres are asserted here.
Permanganate-iron endpoint and blank model
Words: 420
Permanganate-iron titration OurBigBook.com
The apparatus and motivating measurement are described in permanganate-iron titration; the following is an original account of its possible errors. Assume correct titrant standardization, the acidic permanganate-iron balance, quantitative conversion of the sampled Fe2+, and additive contributions expressed as equivalent titrant volumes. Write
V=VFe​+Bs​+Ds​+A+I,Vb​=Bb​+Db​,VFe​=5cnFe​​.
(29)
Here V is the sample titre, Vb​ the titration blank, Bs​,Bb​ background reagent consumption, and Ds​,Db​ signed offsets of the observed titration endpoints from the respective stoichiometry conditions after background consumption. The subscripts distinguish sample and blank. I is additional sample-specific permanganate demand, absent from the blank; A is apparent delivery used to fill an initially air-containing burette tip rather than enter the flask. Assume the blank's tip is already filled; the sample should also have A=0 after proper preparation. These terms are a diagnostic model, not measured components of the stipulated 0.10mL blank.
Subtracting the two accounts proves the error relation
nFe​=5c(V−Vb​)=nFe​+5cΔV,ΔV=(Bs​−Bb​)+(Ds​−Db​)+A+I.
(30)
The simple inference is valid when this residual is negligible. Matching water and sulfuric acid tests the background terms, but does not by itself establish Ds​=Db​: flask composition and viewing conditions can differ. A coloured sample can mask residual permanganate, changing the assigned titration endpoint without a corresponding redox consumption. A sample-specific reducing agent instead contributes positive I by consuming permanganate. A reagent titration blank cannot measure either effect just by omitting the sample.
A transient purple streak before mixing is not the mixed-flask titration endpoint. Conversely, the equivalence point is the five-to-one inventory match, without a promised visible flag. In the ideal selective model, a persistent excess colour requires some permanganate beyond that match. No particular drop size, waiting time or endpoint offset is stipulated here; the same stated colour criterion must be applied to sample and blank, and its transferability checked.
The model also predicts error direction. If a tip bubble disappears during sample delivery, A>0 makes the inferred amount of substance too high because final minus initial burette reading includes liquid that stayed in the tip. Conditioning the tip before the first reading prevents this particular discrepancy; subtracting a separate titration blank is not an instrument repair. Repeated aliquots test scatter, a known added Fe2+ inventory tests the five-to-one response, and an independent titrant standardization tests c. These are the proposed controls from permanganate-iron titration, with distinct diagnostic roles; none alone proves absence of all sample interference.

Saponification

Words: 639 Articles: 2
Hydrolysis OurBigBook.com
Saponification is hydrolysis of an ester under basic conditions. The conductometric saponification assay follows ethyl acetate consumption by hydroxide, producing ethanol and an acetate ion; its equal-starting-concentration case provides a practical second-order reaction example.
Saponification is ester hydrolysis promoted by a chemical base, with net consumption of hydroxide to form a carboxylate and an alcohol. For a carboxylic acid-derived ester, the net chemical equation is
RCOOR′+OH−⟶RCOO−+R′OH.
(31)
The hydroxide is a reactant, rather than merely a regenerated catalyst.[ref]
For ethyl acetate, the balanced chemical equation becomes
CH3​COOC2​H5​+OH−⟶CH3​COO−+C2​H5​OH.
(32)
Both sides contain four carbon chemical atoms, nine hydrogen chemical atoms, three oxygen chemical atoms, and net electric charge −1. A sodium ion supplied by sodium hydroxide is a spectator ion; the net ionic equation omits it without losing electric charge conservation.
In the usual reaction mechanism, hydroxide adds to the carbonyl group, making a reaction intermediate. Departure of the alcohol's conjugate base gives a carboxylic acid; transfer of a proton then gives the carboxylate and the alcohol. Subsequent addition of a chemical acid gives the carboxylic acid by protonation:
RCOO−+H3​O+⟶RCOOH+H2​O.
(33)
This separate acidification changes the reaction product's protonation state.[ref]
The conductometric saponification assay makes hydroxide consumption observable. A university procedure equilibrates separate ethyl acetate and sodium hydroxide stocks in constant-temperature baths, then mixes them in a rinsed conductivity cell. Two platinum electrodes and an alternating-voltage Wheatstone bridge supply an electrical resistance readout. A matched sodium hydroxide–water dilution checks the initial signal; potassium chloride calibrates the cell constant. Replacing hydroxide with less mobile acetate ions lowers electrical conductance, supporting an inference about changing concentration. The manual supplies a procedure rather than measured outcomes. Temperature drift or additional ions can change the signal; it cannot alone identify the full reaction mechanism.[ref]

Saponification with limiting hydroxide

Saponification OurBigBook.com
Consider a hypothetical closed, well mixed chemical solution initially containing 20mmol of ethyl acetate, 12mmol of hydroxide, and no acetate ions or ethanol. One millimole is 10−3 mole. Assume complete conversion as far as the one-to-one chemical equation allows, with no competing chemical reactions. This is an ideal stoichiometry calculation, not a measured yield.
Let the extent of reaction be ξ, expressed in millimoles. The four values of amount of substance, in the order ethyl acetate, hydroxide, acetate ion, ethanol, are
(20−ξ,12−ξ,ξ,ξ)mmol,0≤ξ≤12.
(34)
The upper bound follows because both reactant quantities must be nonnegative. Thus hydroxide is the limiting reagent, and the ideal endpoint ξ=12 leaves
8mmol ethyl acetate,0mmol hydroxide,12mmol acetate,12mmol ethanol.
(35)
The carboxylate formed equals the hydroxide consumed, while unreacted ester remains. Adding more hydroxide raises the stoichiometry bound; merely waiting longer does not change that bound. To convert these values of amount of substance into concentrations, a volume is also required. The endpoint does not specify the reaction rate or time needed to approach it.

Saponification OurBigBook.com
A triglyceride contains three ester linkages joining glycerol to fatty acid-derived acyl groups. Complete saponification therefore consumes three hydroxide equivalents per triglyceride, yielding one glycerol and three fatty acid carboxylates.[ref]
Writing the three hydrocarbon groups separately allows their compositions to differ:
​C3​H5​[OC(=O)R1​][OC(=O)R2​][OC(=O)R3​]+3OH−⟶C3​H5​(OH)3​+R1​COO−+R2​COO−+R3​COO−.​
(36)
This is the preceding ester chemical equation applied three times: each linkage supplies one carboxylate, and each formerly esterified oxygen on the glycerol scaffold gains one hydrogen. The two sides retain the same three Ri​ groups and have net electric charge −3.
Soap consists of sodium or potassium salts of long-chain fatty acids. Its carboxylate head is hydrophilic, while its long hydrocarbon tail is hydrophobic. This makes it an amphiphile and a surfactant: the tails can associate with grease while the heads remain exposed to water, helping disperse grease for rinsing. An acetate ion is also a carboxylate, but lacks the long hydrophobic tail that gives soap this cleaning role.[ref]

Energy coupling (ΔGnet​=ΔG1​+ΔG2​)

Words: 415
Chemical reaction OurBigBook.com
Energy coupling links an endergonic reaction to an exergonic reaction through a reaction mechanism, so that the combined transformation has a favourable change in Gibbs free energy. ATP hydrolysis is a common driving chemical reaction. A shared reaction intermediate, produced in one step and consumed in another, can physically connect the transformations; merely placing two independent chemical reactions in the same chemical solution does not establish energy coupling. See Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell: coupled reactions and activated intermediates.
For a computed example, stipulate an endergonic reaction A⟶B with ΔG1∘′​=+20kJmol−1 under precisely the same biochemical standard state conditions as the quoted ATP hydrolysis value. Assume a reaction mechanism couples one ATP hydrolysis to each A-to-B conversion. The formal sum is
AATP+H2​OA+ATP+H2​O​⟶B,⟶ADP+Pi​,⟶B+ADP+Pi​,​ΔG1∘′​ΔG2∘′​ΔGnet∘′​​=+20kJmol−1,=−30.5kJmol−1,=−10.5kJmol−1.​
(37)
The sum +20+(−30.5)=−10.5 gives an exergonic reaction. The +20 is a chosen teaching value, not a measured property of an identified substance. Outside these reference conditions, add the actual ΔG1​ and ΔG2​, each evaluated using consistent thermodynamic activities; mixing a standard value for one chemical reaction with an unrelated cellular value for the other gives no justified prediction.
Why do the changes in Gibbs free energy add? Gibbs free energy is a state function. Adding consistent reaction changes cancels any shared reaction intermediate and leaves the difference between the combined reactants and combined reaction products. This explains the thermodynamic accounting; it does not construct the reaction mechanism. In many ATP-dependent routes, phosphorylation transfers a phosphate group to a substrate or an enzyme, and subsequent transformation consumes that modified material. The shared material is what connects the steps. Other reaction mechanisms use ATP differently. See Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell: ATP-driven biosynthesis.
The useful achievement is that a common regenerated nucleotide can connect many different processes in metabolism. The net negative change in Gibbs free energy permits the coupled conversion, but supplies no reaction rate: enzymes can lower activation energy barriers without changing the endpoint difference. Energy coupling changes which overall chemical reaction is being considered; catalysis accelerates an available route. See OpenStax Biology 2e, 6.2: free-energy changes and reaction barriers.
A historical landmark is Fritz Lipmann's [ref]. Its sections on the phosphate cycle, generation and utilization of phosphate-bond energy, and group transfer organized these processes around a reusable chemical carrier. The historical terminology should be read with the modern distinction between net hydrolysis and the cost of breaking a chemical bond.

Chemical equation

Words: 346 Articles: 1
Chemical reaction OurBigBook.com
A chemical equation represents a chemical reaction using chemical formulas, with reactants on the left and reaction products on the right. A balanced chemical equation has the same number of chemical atoms of each chemical element on both sides. For molecular hydrogen and molecular oxygen forming water,
2H2​+O2​⟶2H2​O.
(38)
The coefficients 2,1,2 give the relative numbers of molecules; the coefficient 1 is normally omitted. Count hydrogen as 2×2=4 on the left and 2×2=4 on the right, and oxygen as 1×2=2 on the left and 2×1=2 on the right. See Flowers et al., Chemistry 2e, §4.1: writing and balancing chemical equations.
To balance the initial expression H2​+O2​⟶H2​O, first put 2 before water to match the two oxygen chemical atoms. This creates four hydrogen chemical atoms on the right, so put 2 before molecular hydrogen. Changing a coefficient multiplies the entire chemical formula. Changing a subscript changes composition and usually the chemical substance: 2H2​O is two water molecules, whereas H2​O2​ is one hydrogen peroxide molecule. Never balance a chemical equation by changing its subscripts.
The bookkeeping follows from conservation of the atomic nuclei in ordinary, non-nuclear chemical reactions; chemical bonds and the distribution of electrons can change. For a chemical equation involving ions, total electric charge must also match. For example, the existing self-ionization of water equation has zero total electric charge on each side, since the +1 of hydronium cancels the −1 of hydroxide. See 2.6 Ionic and Molecular Compounds (§2.6: nuclei and ions).
The same 2:1:2 ratio relates changes in amount of substance: two moles of molecular hydrogen consumed per mole of molecular oxygen correspond to two moles of water formed. A mole is a defined unit, not one molecule; the little whole-number picture is an abstract counting model, not a claim that a macroscopic sample contains just five molecules. See molecular count and amount of substance for the exact conversion and SI base unit: mole by Bureau International des Poids et Mesures for the definition.
This is why a balanced chemical equation is useful: stoichiometry turns the same atom accounting into relations between measurable quantities. It does not determine reaction rate, the final conversion set by chemical equilibrium, or the actual yield of recovered reaction products. The limiting reagent gives an upper bound under the specified chemical reaction.

Stoichiometry (νi​)

Words: 619 Articles: 5
Chemical reaction OurBigBook.com
Stoichiometry relates the quantities consumed and formed in a chemical reaction. Its coefficients are ratios of entity counts, or equivalently of amount of substance, rather than ratios of masses. For the water chemical equation, consuming two molecular hydrogen molecules per molecular oxygen molecule gives the same 2:1 ratio as consuming two moles of molecular hydrogen per mole of molecular oxygen. Multiplying every entity count by the same factor preserves the ratio. See Flowers et al., Chemistry 2e, reaction stoichiometry.
Coefficients and subscripts do different jobs. The coefficient in 2H2​O counts two water molecules; the subscript says that each contains two hydrogen chemical atoms. Changing coefficients scales quantities. Changing a subscript changes the specified chemical substance.
This distinction catches a common counting error: one mole of water molecules contains two moles of hydrogen chemical atoms and one mole of oxygen chemical atoms. Always specify what is counted.
Stoichiometry records reactant and product multiplicities in a chemical reaction or a chemical reaction network. The change caused by one reaction is its stoichiometric vector; multiplying by the reaction rate gives its contribution to the concentration equations. For two identical reactants the rate-constant convention absorbs any combinatorial factor.

Stoichiometry OurBigBook.com
For a closed system with one specified chemical reaction, the extent of reaction ξ records progress from ξ=0 through ni​=ni,0​+νi​ξ. Here ni​ is the amount of substance of species i, and the signed stoichiometric vector has negative entries for reactants and positive entries for reaction products. For the water chemical equation in the order H2​,O2​,H2​O, it is (−2,−1,2). The normalization of ξ depends on the chosen coefficients. See IUPAC Gold Book, extent of reaction.
With particle numbers instead of molar amounts, a molecular extent ξN​ obeys dNi​=νi​dξN​, and the chemical potentials are measured per particle. At fixed temperature and volume, the Helmholtz free energy then satisfies dF=(∑i​νi​μi​)dξN​. An interior chemical equilibrium requires ∑i​νi​μi​=0; the molar convention gives the same relation with chemical potentials per mole.

Limiting reagent

Words: 198
Stoichiometry OurBigBook.com
The limiting reagent is the reactant exhausted first if the specified chemical reaction proceeds to the maximum conversion permitted by stoichiometry. With initial values of amount of substance ni,0​ for the reactants and positive consumption coefficients ai​, the largest forward extent of reaction is ξmax​=mini​(ni,0​/ai​). Compare these quotients, rather than simply choosing the smallest initial quantity. This calculation predicts the maximum reaction product quantity and identifies which reactant supply must increase to raise it. See Flowers et al., Chemistry 2e, limiting reactants.
Start with 3mol of molecular hydrogen, 1mol of molecular oxygen and no water. Assume complete conversion by the displayed chemical reaction, without competing reactions. Then
ξmax​=min(23mol​,11mol​)=1mol.
(40)
The molecular oxygen is the limiting reagent. Consumption of 2mol of molecular hydrogen and 1mol of molecular oxygen forms 2mol of water, leaving 1mol of molecular hydrogen. Initially there are 1.806642228×1024 molecular hydrogen molecules and 6.02214076×1023 molecular oxygen molecules; after conversion there are 1.204428152×1024 water molecules and 6.02214076×1023 leftover molecular hydrogen molecules.
As a check, the initial inventory has 6mol of hydrogen chemical atoms and 2mol of oxygen chemical atoms. The final water contains 4mol of hydrogen chemical atoms, and leftover molecular hydrogen supplies the remaining 2mol. The atom totals balance even though the total amount of substance of molecules falls from four to three moles.

Mutarotation

Words: 17
Chemical reaction OurBigBook.com
Mutarotation is a change in optical rotation as anomers interconvert in a chemical solution. The glucose mutarotation experiment detects redistribution between cyclic forms through monosaccharide ring-chain interconversion.
